title: Foundations of Cognitive Psychology
description: The cognitive revolution, the mind as information processor, and how cognition is studied

concepts.title: The Cognitive Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
For the first half of the twentieth century, mainstream American psychology was dominated by behaviourism (Watson, Skinner), which insisted that only observable stimulus-response relations were proper objects of science. Mental processes were dismissed as a 'black box' that could not be studied rigorously.

In the 1950s a coalition of dissatisfied researchers launched what George Miller later called the cognitive revolution. Key milestones include Noam Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior, which argued that language could not be reduced to conditioning; Miller's 1956 paper 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two' on memory capacity; and Ulric Neisser's 1967 textbook Cognitive Psychology, which named and defined the new field.

The shift was driven partly by the arrival of the digital computer, which offered a new metaphor: the mind as an information-processing system with internal representations and operations.

concepts.title: The Information-Processing Framework
concepts.contentHtml:
Cognitive psychology models the mind as a sequence of stages that encode, store, transform, and retrieve information. A perceived stimulus is converted into a mental representation, manipulated by various processes, and produces a response.

Donald Broadbent's Perception and Communication (1958) gave one of the first explicit flow diagrams: sensory inputs pass through a limited-capacity filter, then enter short-term memory, and may be transferred to long-term storage. Atkinson and Shiffrin's modal model (1968) refined this into the famous sensory–short-term–long-term architecture.

The framework introduced concepts that remain central: capacity limits, parallel vs. serial processing, top-down (concept-driven) and bottom-up (data-driven) processing, and the distinction between structure (the architecture) and process (what the architecture does).

concepts.title: How Cognition Is Studied
concepts.contentHtml:
Because mental processes cannot be observed directly, cognitive psychologists infer them from carefully measured behaviour. Key methods include:

Reaction time (chronometry): Franciscus Donders (1868) showed that subtracting simple reaction times from choice reaction times estimates the duration of a decision stage. Sternberg's memory-scanning task (1966) used reaction time slopes to argue for serial exhaustive search.

Accuracy and error patterns: systematic mistakes reveal underlying mechanisms — for example, confusing 'B' and 'V' in immediate recall suggests acoustic coding in short-term memory (Conrad, 1964).

Neuropsychology: patients like H.M., who lost the ability to form new long-term memories after bilateral hippocampal removal in 1953, dissociate memory systems that look unified in healthy people.

Neuroimaging: PET and fMRI from the 1990s let researchers correlate cognitive tasks with brain activation, complementing behavioural data.

title: Attention
description: Selective filtering, feature integration, and the limits of awareness

concepts.title: Selective Attention and the Filter
concepts.contentHtml:
The classic problem of attention is the cocktail party: how do we follow one conversation in a noisy room? Colin Cherry's dichotic listening experiments (1953) presented different messages to each ear and asked listeners to shadow (repeat aloud) one channel. Listeners could report almost nothing about the unattended channel — not even a switch from English to German — though physical features like a change in voice pitch were noticed.

Donald Broadbent's filter theory (1958) explained this with an early, all-or-nothing filter that selected one channel by physical properties before any meaning was extracted.

Anne Treisman's attenuation theory (1960) softened the filter: unattended channels are dampened rather than blocked, which is why your own name pops out when whispered across the room. Deutsch and Deutsch (1963) went further with a late selection model in which everything is processed semantically and attention selects only at the response stage.

concepts.title: Visual Attention and Feature Integration
concepts.contentHtml:
Anne Treisman's Feature Integration Theory (1980) explained visual search. Simple features like colour, orientation, and motion are detected in parallel across the whole visual field — finding a red dot among green ones is fast and roughly independent of the number of distractors (a pop-out).

Combinations of features require focal attention to bind them into objects. Searching for a red vertical line among red horizontals and green verticals is slow and scales with display size: you must inspect items roughly one at a time.

Michael Posner's cueing paradigm (1980) showed that attention can be deployed without eye movements. A peripheral cue speeds detection at the cued location and slows it elsewhere, demonstrating a covert spotlight. Posner's work also distinguished networks for alerting, orienting, and executive control.

concepts.title: Inattentional and Change Blindness
concepts.contentHtml:
Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's invisible gorilla study (1999) asked viewers to count basketball passes between players in white shirts. Roughly half failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene, beating their chest, and exiting. This is inattentional blindness: without attention, even salient objects can fail to reach awareness.

Change blindness, demonstrated by Ronald Rensink and others in the 1990s, shows that large changes between two alternating images go unnoticed when separated by a brief flicker that masks local motion signals. We have a strong intuition that we see the world richly and continuously, but the visual system retains far less than it feels.

These phenomena support a key cognitive lesson: perception is selective. Awareness is not a faithful video of the world — it is constructed from whatever fragments attention has bound together.

title: Memory Systems
description: Working memory, long-term memory, and how the architecture of memory was discovered

concepts.title: Short-Term Memory and the Modal Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Atkinson and Shiffrin's modal model (1968) proposed three stores: a brief sensory register, a limited-capacity short-term store, and a vast long-term store. Information is rehearsed in short-term memory and gradually transferred to long-term storage.

George Miller's 'The Magical Number Seven' (1956) argued that short-term capacity is roughly seven items, but that chunking — grouping items into meaningful units — radically expands effective capacity. The string F-B-I-C-I-A-N-A-S-A is ten items as letters but three as agencies.

The Brown–Peterson task (1959) showed that short-term memory decays within about 18 seconds when rehearsal is prevented by a distractor task like counting backward. Conrad (1964) found that recall errors in short-term memory tend to be acoustic ('B' for 'V') even when items are presented visually, suggesting a phonological code.

concepts.title: Baddeley's Working Memory
concepts.contentHtml:
Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974) replaced the unitary short-term store with working memory: an active system for holding and manipulating information during cognition.

The model has three original components and a later addition. The phonological loop stores speech-based material and refreshes it via subvocal rehearsal — its capacity is limited by what can be rehearsed in roughly two seconds (the word-length effect). The visuospatial sketchpad handles visual and spatial information. The central executive is an attentional controller that coordinates the slave systems and switches between tasks.

Baddeley added the episodic buffer (2000) to integrate information from the loop, sketchpad, and long-term memory into coherent episodes.

Working memory capacity correlates with reading comprehension, fluid intelligence, and academic performance — making it one of the most predictive variables in cognitive psychology.

concepts.title: Long-Term Memory: Tulving's Distinctions
concepts.contentHtml:
Endel Tulving (1972, 1985) argued that long-term memory is not one system but several. Within declarative (consciously accessible) memory he distinguished episodic memory — memory for specific events tied to a time and place ('what I had for breakfast yesterday') — from semantic memory — general knowledge about the world ('Paris is the capital of France').

Procedural memory, by contrast, is non-declarative: knowing how to ride a bicycle or type without being able to articulate the rules.

Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), whose hippocampi were removed in 1953 to treat epilepsy, lost the ability to form new declarative memories but could still acquire new motor skills, dissociating the systems neurologically. Patients with semantic dementia, by contrast, lose general knowledge while retaining recent personal events.

Tulving's framework is now standard, supported by decades of behavioural, neuropsychological, and imaging evidence.

title: Reasoning, Heuristics, and Biases
description: Dual-process theory and the systematic ways human reasoning departs from logic

concepts.title: Dual-Process Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Daniel Kahneman's synthesis in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) popularised the dual-process view that has been developing since Wason and Evans in the 1970s.

System 1 is fast, automatic, effortless, parallel, and largely unconscious. It produces immediate impressions, perceptions, intuitions, and feelings. Reading a simple word, recognising a face, or driving on an empty road are System 1 tasks.

System 2 is slow, deliberate, effortful, serial, and capacity-limited. It performs explicit reasoning, computation, and self-control. Multiplying 17 by 24, parking in a tight space, or weighing arguments are System 2 tasks.

System 1 runs constantly and supplies System 2 with proposals; System 2 endorses, modifies, or overrides them. Because System 2 is lazy and effortful, it often accepts System 1's outputs uncritically — which is the source of many systematic errors.

concepts.title: Heuristics and Biases
concepts.contentHtml:
Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, beginning in the early 1970s, demonstrated that people use mental shortcuts — heuristics — that work well in many situations but produce predictable errors in others.

The availability heuristic judges frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid plane crashes make air travel feel riskier than driving even though statistics say otherwise.

The representativeness heuristic judges probability by similarity to a stereotype. The Linda problem (1983) found that most people rate 'Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller' — a violation of basic probability called the conjunction fallacy.

Anchoring: an initial value biases subsequent estimates even when irrelevant. Spinning a wheel of numbers shifted estimates of African UN membership in Tversky and Kahneman's classic demonstration.

concepts.title: Logical Reasoning and Confirmation Bias
concepts.contentHtml:
Peter Wason's selection task (1966) presents four cards (A, K, 4, 7) and a rule: 'If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.' Which cards must you turn over to test the rule? The logically correct answer is A and 7 (to check for a counterexample), but most participants pick A and 4 — looking for confirming instances.

This illustrates confirmation bias: a tendency to seek and weight evidence that supports existing beliefs and to discount contradictions. Wason's earlier 2-4-6 task showed the same pattern in inductive reasoning.

Curiously, performance on the selection task improves dramatically when the same logical structure is framed in social or deontic terms ('If a person is drinking alcohol, they must be over 18'). Leda Cosmides argued this reveals a specialised cheater detection module shaped by evolution. Whether or not that explanation is correct, content effects show that human reasoning is not a content-blind logic engine.

title: Language, Problem Solving, and Expertise
description: How the mind handles structured knowledge: from linguistic competence to expert insight

concepts.title: Language and Mental Representation
concepts.contentHtml:
Noam Chomsky's Syntactic Structures (1957) argued that linguistic competence cannot be a stockpile of memorised sentences — speakers routinely produce and understand novel utterances. Language must be governed by an internalised generative grammar capable of infinite use of finite means.

Chomsky's poverty of the stimulus argument noted that children acquire complex syntax from limited and often degenerate input, suggesting innate constraints — a language acquisition device or universal grammar.

At the lexical level, words map onto mental concepts. Eleanor Rosch's prototype theory (1975) showed that category membership is graded: a robin is a 'better' bird than a penguin. Categorisation is fast and graded, not all-or-nothing.

Reading and listening also depend on top-down processes: the McGurk effect shows that seeing lips form 'ga' while hearing 'ba' produces an integrated percept of 'da' — perception is multimodal and inferential.

concepts.title: Mental Imagery and Problem Solving
concepts.contentHtml:
Roger Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler's mental rotation studies (1971) asked whether two three-dimensional shapes shown at different angles were the same. Reaction time increased linearly with the angular difference, suggesting that participants were rotating an internal analogue representation at a roughly constant rate. Imagery, the data implied, shares structure with perception.

Problem solving was studied by the Gestalt psychologists (Köhler, Duncker) and reframed by Newell and Simon's Human Problem Solving (1972), which described problems as a search through a problem space using operators that transform states.

Functional fixedness (Duncker's candle problem, 1945) is the failure to use a familiar object in a novel way — participants struggle to mount a candle on a wall using a tack box because they see the box only as a container. Insight problems often require restructuring the representation rather than incremental search, producing the famous 'aha!' experience.

concepts.title: Schemas, Expertise, and Embodied Cognition
concepts.contentHtml:
Frederic Bartlett's Remembering (1932) showed that recall is not literal playback but reconstruction guided by schemas — organised packets of prior knowledge. Participants reading the Native American folktale 'The War of the Ghosts' systematically distorted unfamiliar elements into culturally expected forms.

Schemas are also central to expertise. Adriaan de Groot (1946) and later William Chase and Herbert Simon (1973) showed that chess masters recall briefly viewed positions far better than novices — but only when the pieces are arranged in plausible game configurations. With random positions, the advantage vanishes. Expertise is large libraries of meaningful chunks, not raw memory power.

Recent embodied cognition approaches (Barsalou, Lakoff) argue that abstract concepts are partly grounded in perceptual and motor experience: understanding 'grasp the idea' recruits some of the same circuitry as grasping with the hand. Cognition, on this view, is not pure symbol manipulation isolated from body and world.
